content.text:
I'm trying to arrive at the right way to use the `wakil` product.  This product has self-contained skills and a mechanism for overriding those skills by the user working with it.  Ideally I would want to be running tasks within a kb using the Hermes agent that has been customized with the functionality in Wakil.  That said, I would prefer to not simply copy every skill into hermes because it updates skills as it learns (indeed, I'd like Hermes to leverage the mechanism for overriding Wakil skills, so that it's clear what it has changed). 

That said, I'm not sure if I'm understanding how Hermes and Agents generally integrate with tools like Wakil.  So, given that, I'm looking for significant guidance (and possible correction) on what I'm doing.  Ask me questions to help me gain clarity on what I'm trying to do.

(Note -- there's another agent currently working on refactoring skills, so those files may change while you work).

input.description: Explore wakil skills and override mechanism
input.prompt:
I'm exploring the `wakil` repo (a local-first Python CLI agent for a personal Markdown knowledge base, per CLAUDE.md at repo root) to understand its "skills" system and how skill overrides work.

Context: another agent may be mid-refactor of the skills code right now, so files could shift under you — focus on understanding the current *architecture/mechanism* (how skills are defined, discovered, loaded, and overridden) rather than memorizing exact line numbers, and note if something looks mid-refactor or inconsistent.

Please investigate and report back (be thorough, this is "very thorough" breadth):

1. Where do "skills" live in this codebase (directory structure, file format — e.g. Markdown with frontmatter, Python modules, YAML, etc.)? Is there a distinction between built-in/self-contained skills shipped with wakil vs. user-level overrides?
2. What mechanism exists (if any) for a user (or another agent) to override/customize a built-in skill? E.g., is there a precedence order (project-level vs user-level vs global), a specific directory like `.wakil/skills/` or `~/.wakil/skills/`, or a config file that controls resolution order? Look for any docs, README, or code comments describing "skill resolution."
3. Is there any concept of "layering" or "diffing" a skill override against the original — i.e., does wakil track *what changed* between a base skill and an override, or is an override simply a full replacement file that shadows the original?
4. Are skills invoked by a CLI command, an MCP server exposed to external agents, a Python API, or something else? How would an *external* agent (running outside this repo, e.g. a separate agent tool) actually invoke or make use of a wakil skill?
5. Search for any references to "Hermes" anywhere in this repo (code, docs, commit messages, issue trackers) — the user mentioned an agent called "Hermes" that they want to use wakil's functionality from. Report exactly what you find, even if nothing.
6. Look for any docs (README.md, docs/, ADRs via any adr directory, CONTRIBUTING.md) that describe the intended integration story between wakil and external agent frontends/runtimes.

For each finding, cite the file path. If the skill-resolution mechanism doesn't exist yet (e.g., it's aspirational/planned but not implemented), say so clearly and point to where it's discussed as a plan (e.g. a design doc or TODO) versus actually implemented in code.

Report back in a structured way covering all 6 points, under 600 words plus file citations.

1	# Wakil
2	
3	> [!NOTE]
4	> **wakīl** /wa-KĪL/
5	> *noun* · Arabic **وكيل**
6	>
7	> 1. **An entrusted agent;** one authorized to act on another’s behalf.
8	> 2. **A representative, deputy, or proxy** whose role rests not merely on action, but on conferred trust.
9	> 3. **One who carries responsibility for another’s interests**, standing in the space between delegation and reliance.
10	>
11	> *From Arabic roots associated with entrusting, relying upon, and placing confidence in another.*
12	
13	`wakil` is a local-first Python CLI agent for working with a personal Markdown
14	knowledge base (GBrain / Obsidian style): ingest, search, connect, revise, and
15	reason over Markdown notes. Markdown is the source of truth; SQLite is the
16	operational index; git provides history and review. See `PROMPT.md` for the
17	full plan and `TODO.md` for what's next.
18	
19	## Install
20	
21	Requires Python 3.12+ and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).
22	
23	```bash
24	uv sync
25	```
26	
27	## Usage
28	
29	```bash
30	# Initialize a knowledge-base workspace (creates .wakil/ with config + SQLite db,
31	# and registers the workspace name for -w lookups)
32	uv run wakil init ~/kb --name kb
33	
34	# Show workspace status: notes indexed, git state, QMD availability
35	uv run wakil -w ~/kb status
36	
37	# Re-index Markdown files after edits
38	uv run wakil -w kb index
39	
40	# Search the knowledge base (QMD if installed, plus local FTS indexes)
41	uv run wakil -w kb search "insurance claims routing"
42	
43	# Ask a grounded question (requires a model provider, see below)
44	uv run wakil -w kb query "How do my notes on FNOL relate to graph memory?"
45	
46	# Step 1 — capture raw material (deterministic, no model)
47	uv run wakil -w kb ingest transcript ./raw/meeting.txt \
48	    --context "Attendees: Jane Doe, Bob (Acme Corp). Weekly claims sync."
49	uv run wakil -w kb ingest article https://example.com/post
50	uv run wakil -w kb ingest text ./clipping.md
51	
52	# Step 2 — analyze the captured source and link it into the KB
53	uv run wakil -w kb enrich 1
54	
55	# Git-native ingest: commit on a wakil/ingest/* branch, optionally open a PR
56	uv run wakil -w kb ingest transcript ./raw/meeting.txt --branch
57	uv run wakil -w kb ingest article https://example.com/post --pr
58	
59	# Git awareness
60	uv run wakil -w kb git summary
61	uv run wakil -w kb git history concepts/graph-memory.md
62	
63	# Memory lifecycle
64	uv run wakil -w kb memory list --state candidate
65	uv run wakil -w kb memory show 3
66	uv run wakil -w kb memory promote 3 7
67	uv run wakil -w kb memory reject 4
68	uv run wakil -w kb memory archive 1
69	```
70	
71	## Memory lifecycle
72	
73	Ingests propose memories in `candidate` state; you review and decide:
74	
75	    working → candidate → durable
76	                      ↘ rejected
77	    durable → archived
78	
79	`wakil memory list` (with `--state`/`--type` filters) reviews them, `promote`
80	moves them to durable, `reject` removes them from search, and `archive` keeps
81	them searchable but downranked. Invalid transitions are refused. Rather than
82	deleting, retrieval fades memories: durable ranks first, then candidate, then
83	working (fading further after 30 days), then archived. Memories used to
84	answer a query get their `last_seen_at` bumped for future ranking.
85	
86	## Selecting a workspace
87	
88	Every command accepts a global `-w`/`--workspace` option (before the
89	subcommand) naming the workspace to operate on:
90	
91	- **omitted** — use the current directory, searching upward for a `.wakil/`
92	  workspace (so any subdirectory of the knowledge base works);
93	- **a directory** — use that path (also searched upward);
94	- **a name** — look up a workspace registered by `wakil init` in
95	  `~/.config/wakil/workspaces.yaml`, so `wakil -w kb status` works from
96	  anywhere.
97	
98	The `WAKIL_WORKSPACE` environment variable provides the same value as a
99	default, e.g. `export WAKIL_WORKSPACE=kb`.
100	
101	## Skills
102	
103	A skill is a directory containing a `SKILL.md` file (Claude-Skills-compatible
104	frontmatter: `name`, `skill_api`, optional `version`), plus any supporting
105	files it needs. wakil resolves a skill name by searching, in order,
106	`WAKIL_SKILL_PATH` (a `:`-separated list of extra roots), then
107	`<kb-root>/skills`, then `~/.config/wakil/skills`, then built-in skills — the
108	first directory found wins, and a broken override blocks fallback rather than
109	being silently skipped.
110	
111	```bash
112	uv run wakil -w kb skills list                       # effective name + source
113	uv run wakil -w kb skills which meeting-synthesis -v  # selected path, roots, shadows
114	uv run wakil -w kb skills validate                    # check every root and skill
115	```
116	
117	## Ingest
118	
119	Ingest is two explicit steps.
120	
121	**Step 1 — capture** (`wakil ingest transcript|text|article`) is fully
122	deterministic; no model is involved. Text is extracted (transcripts get light
123	cleanup: bracketed and line-leading timestamps removed, whitespace normalized
124	— never model rewriting), deduped by content hash, and written under
125	`sources/` as a raw capture. Transcript frontmatter follows the KB schema:
126	if `SCHEMA.md` contains a yaml template in a transcript/source section, its
127	fields are used (known fields like the meeting date and create date are
128	filled in); otherwise exactly two fields are written — `created` and
129	`meeting_date` (inferred from the filename or the transcript's opening
130	lines). `--context`/`-C` accepts a few lines about the source (attendees,
131	company, purpose) and is stored on the source record for step 2.
132	
133	**Step 2 — enrichment** (`wakil enrich <source-id>`) is a fixed,
134	code-sequenced pipeline of two model calls, one preview, one confirm:
135	
136	1. **Extraction** — judgment prose from `skills/<kind>/SKILL.md` (transcript,
137	   article, or text) produces the summary, key points, candidate memories
138	   (dated events carry their own `event_date`), relationships, and a proposed
139	   KB note. The capture-time context (or a fresh `--context`) plus the
140	   opening of the source drive a search for related entity notes and prior
141	   meetings, which the model links with [[wikilinks]].
142	   `SCHEMA.md`/`RESOLVER.md` guidance is included so the note follows the
143	   KB's page shape and routing rules.
144	2. **Entity resolution** — always invoked, never optional: for each entity
145	   the source touched, the model decides create/update/skip against the
146	   existing notes and the shipped entity schemas. Notable new entities
147	   (action `create`) become stub pages with schema-valid frontmatter and a
148	   Compiled Truth / Timeline skeleton, routed into the type's canonical
149	   directory; the decisions are shown in the preview before anything is
150	   written.
151	
152	Model output is validated against Pydantic contracts (the same JSON Schema
153	shown to the model), retried once on a validation failure, and fails visibly
154	— never silently coerced. Before apply, `validate_proposal()` checks every
155	proposed file's frontmatter against the entity schemas; a proposed `type:`
156	with no schema is a hard stop, not a best-guess write. Re-running requires
157	`--force`.
158	
159	Both steps preview before writing (`--yes` skips the prompt) and accept
160	`--branch`/`--commit`/`--pr`; captures commit as `wakil source:`, enrichment
161	as `wakil ingest:`. Proposed notes fall back to `drafts/` when routing is
162	unclear or the path collides; existing files are never overwritten. Extracted
163	memories are stored as `candidate` state for review with `wakil memory`.
164	
165	## Git-native changes
166	
167	When the knowledge base is a git repository, ingest can make its changes
168	reviewable git history:
169	
170	- `--commit`/`-c` commits the ingested files on the current branch, staging
171	  only the files wakil wrote (your other uncommitted work is untouched);
172	- `--branch`/`-b` first checks the working tree is clean, then creates a
173	  `wakil/ingest/<date>-<slug>` branch and commits there;
174	- `--pr` additionally pushes the branch and opens a pull request via the
175	  GitHub CLI (`gh`), when it is installed and an `origin` remote exists.
176	
177	Commits follow the wakil conventions (`wakil ingest: add ...`) and every
178	commit is recorded in the workspace database (`git_changes`). `wakil git
179	summary` shows the current branch, pending changes, recent commits, and
180	wakil-created branches; `wakil git history <path>` shows one file's history.
181	
182	## Search
183	
184	`wakil search` combines two engines: [QMD](https://github.com/tobi/qmd) over
185	the Markdown knowledge base when the `qmd` binary is installed (`--mode
186	search|vsearch|query` selects BM25, vector, or hybrid), and SQLite FTS5
187	indexes over note metadata, memories, and sources. QMD results take
188	precedence; FTS fills in workspace records QMD doesn't cover.
189	
190	## Query
191	
192	`wakil query` retrieves matching notes, memories, and sources, sends them to a
193	model as numbered context blocks, and prints a cited answer. Answers are
194	grounded: if the knowledge base doesn't support an answer, wakil says so.
195	Each query is recorded in the workspace database (`query_runs`).
196	
197	Configure a provider via environment variables (see `.env.example`):
198	
199	- `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` — uses Anthropic (default model `claude-opus-4-8`)
200	- `OPENAI_API_KEY` + `WAKIL_MODEL` (+ optional `WAKIL_OPENAI_BASE_URL`) — any
201	  OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including local model servers
202	- `WAKIL_MODEL` / `WAKIL_PROVIDER` — override the model or force a provider
203	
204	`wakil init` indexes every Markdown file in the workspace (title, frontmatter,
205	content hash), detects whether the directory is a git repository, checks for
206	QMD on the PATH, and records high-priority context files (`README.md`,
207	`AGENTS.md`, `SCHEMA.md`, `RESOLVER.md`) when present.
208	
209	## Development
210	
211	```bash
212	uv run pytest       # tests
213	uv run ruff check   # lint
214	```
215

1	# Skill Resolution Specification
2	
3	## 1. Purpose
4	
5	This specification defines how `wakil` discovers, selects, validates, and loads
6	skills.
7	
8	`wakil` ships with built-in skills and allows a single user to replace them with
9	knowledge-base-local or user-level implementations. Resolution follows an
10	ordered search path: the first matching skill wins, and the selected skill
11	directory is loaded as a complete unit.
12	
13	The design favors predictable behavior, useful diagnostics, and a small
14	implementation surface.
15	
16	---
17	
18	## 2. Goals
19	
20	The resolver must:
21	
22	- allow users to override built-in skills without modifying installed files;
23	- support knowledge-base-local and user-level skill overrides;
24	- resolve skills deterministically from a documented precedence order;
25	- load each skill entirely from one directory;
26	- fail clearly when the selected skill is invalid;
27	- make the selected implementation easy to inspect;
28	- preserve local overrides when `wakil` is upgraded.
29	
30	---
31	
32	## 3. Non-goals
33	
34	The initial implementation does not support:
35	
36	- remote skill registries or automatic downloads;
37	- multi-user or organization-level policy;
38	- inheritance or partial file-level overrides;
39	- merging files across skill directories;
40	- skill dependency resolution;
41	- automatic drift detection or merging;
42	- filesystem watching or live reload;
43	- aliases or renamed-skill migration;
44	- execution of arbitrary skill-provided code.
45	
46	---
47	
48	## 4. Skill structure
49	
50	Skills are forward- but not necessarily reverse-compatible with [Claude Skills](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview)
51	
52	A skill is a directory containing a required `SKILL.md` file:
53	
54	```text
55	<skill-root>/
56	    <skill-name>/
57	        SKILL.md
58	```
59	
60	A skill may include supporting files:
61	
62	```text
63	<skill-name>/
64	    SKILL.md
65	    templates/
66	    examples/
67	    references/
68	    schemas/
69	    scripts/
70	```
71	
72	Once a skill directory is selected, all of its files must come from that
73	directory. The resolver must never borrow missing files from a lower-precedence
74	implementation of the same skill.
75	
76	---
77	
78	## 5. Skill names
79	
80	Skill names must use lowercase kebab case:
81	
82	```text
83	meeting-synthesis
84	article-ingestion
85	entity-resolution
86	```
87	
88	A valid name matches:
89	
90	```text
91	[a-z][a-z0-9]*(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*
92	```
93	
94	Names containing path separators, whitespace, uppercase letters, `.` path
95	components, or leading or trailing hyphens are invalid.
96	
97	The directory name is the canonical skill name.
98	
99	---
100	
101	## 6. Skill roots and precedence
102	
103	The resolver searches these roots in order:
104	
105	```text
106	1. Roots supplied through WAKIL_SKILL_PATH
107	2. <kb-root>/skills
108	3. <user-config>/wakil/skills
109	4. Built-in skills
110	```
111	
112	The first matching skill directory is authoritative.
113	
114	For example:
115	
116	```text
117	WAKIL_SKILL_PATH=~/experimental-skills
118	```
119	
120	produces:
121	
122	```text
123	1. ~/experimental-skills
124	2. <kb-root>/skills
125	3. <user-config>/wakil/skills
126	4. <builtin>/skills
127	```
128	
129	The built-in root is always added internally. Users do not include it in
130	`WAKIL_SKILL_PATH`.
131	
132	### 6.1 Knowledge-base-local skills
133	
134	Knowledge-base-local skills live at:
135	
136	```text
137	<kb-root>/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md
138	```
139	
140	They apply only to that knowledge base.
141	
142	### 6.2 User-level skills
143	
144	User-level skills live under the operating system's application configuration
145	directory, for example:
146	
147	```text
148	~/.config/wakil/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md
149	```
150	
151	The actual base directory should be determined through the platform's standard
152	configuration-directory mechanism (e.g. `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`)
153	
154	### 6.3 Additional roots
155	
156	`WAKIL_SKILL_PATH` uses the platform's normal path-list separator:
157	
158	- `:` on Unix-like systems;
159	- `;` on Windows.
160	
161	Empty entries are ignored and must not mean the current working directory.
162	
163	Paths may contain `~` and environment variables. Relative entries are resolved
164	against the current working directory, although absolute paths are recommended.
165	
166	---
167	
168	## 7. Root normalization
169	
170	Before searching, the resolver must:
171	
172	1. expand `~` and environment variables;
173	2. convert paths to absolute normalized paths;
174	3. remove duplicate roots while preserving the first occurrence.
175	
176	Missing default roots, such as `<kb-root>/skills`, are ignored.
177	
178	A path explicitly listed in `WAKIL_SKILL_PATH` that exists but is not a
179	directory is a configuration error. A missing explicit path should produce a
180	warning in normal operation and an error in validation commands.
181	
182	Symbolic links may be followed using normal filesystem behavior. No special
183	symlink policy is required for the initial single-user implementation.
184	
185	---
186	
187	## 8. Skill metadata
188	
189	`SKILL.md` must begin with YAML frontmatter containing:
190	
191	```yaml
192	---
193	name: meeting-synthesis
194	description: Synthesizes a meeting transcript into a structured note.
195	skill_api: 1
196	---
197	```
198	
199	Required fields:
200	
201	- `name`: must exactly match the skill directory name;
202	- `skill_api`: identifies the skill contract expected by the file.
203	
204	Optional fields:
205	
206	```yaml
207	version: 2
208	```
209	
210	`version` is informational. The resolver does not perform semantic-version
211	dependency solving.
212	
213	The initial application supports one explicitly defined `skill_api` version.
214	A skill requiring another version is invalid.
215	
216	---
217	
218	## 9. Resolution behavior
219	
220	To resolve a skill named `meeting-synthesis`, the resolver:
221	
222	1. validates the requested name;
223	2. constructs the ordered skill-root list;
224	3. checks each root for `meeting-synthesis/`;
225	4. selects the first matching directory;
226	5. validates its `SKILL.md`;
227	6. returns the selected skill and its source.
228	
229	The normal execution path may stop after selecting and validating the first
230	match. Diagnostic commands may continue scanning to report shadowed matches.
231	
232	### 9.1 First match wins
233	
234	Given:
235	
236	```text
237	<kb-root>/skills/meeting-synthesis/SKILL.md
238	<builtin>/skills/meeting-synthesis/SKILL.md
239	```
240	
241	the knowledge-base-local implementation is selected.
242	
243	### 9.2 Invalid overrides block fallback
244	
245	If the first matching directory exists but is invalid, resolution fails.
246	
247	Examples:
248	
249	- `SKILL.md` is missing;
250	- frontmatter is malformed;
251	- `name` does not match the directory;
252	- `skill_api` is unsupported;
253	- `SKILL.md` cannot be read.
254	
255	The resolver must not silently fall back to a lower-precedence implementation.
256	A broken override should be visible and corrected rather than ignored.
257	
258	### 9.3 Whole-directory selection
259	
260	Supporting files are resolved relative to the selected skill directory.
261	
262	For example:
263	
264	```text
265	templates/meeting-note.md
266	```
267	
268	means:
269	
270	```text
271	<selected-skill-directory>/templates/meeting-note.md
272	```
273	
274	It does not resolve relative to the knowledge-base root, current working
275	directory, or built-in version of the skill.
276	
277	The resolver does not need to pre-validate every referenced resource. Missing
278	supporting files may be reported when the skill loader or runtime attempts to
279	open them.
280	
281	---
282	
283	## 10. Resolution result
284	
285	A successful resolution should return enough information to load the skill and
286	explain where it came from:
287	
288	```yaml
289	name: meeting-synthesis
290	source: kb-local
291	root: /Users/example/my-kb/skills
292	directory: /Users/example/my-kb/skills/meeting-synthesis
293	manifest: /Users/example/my-kb/skills/meeting-synthesis/SKILL.md
294	metadata:
295	  name: meeting-synthesis
296	  skill_api: 1
297	  version: 2
298	```
299	
300	Required result fields:
301	
302	- canonical skill name;
303	- source type;
304	- selected root;
305	- skill directory;
306	- `SKILL.md` path;
307	- parsed metadata.
308	
309	The core resolver does not need to calculate content hashes or record every
310	shadowed candidate.
311	
312	---
313	
314	## 11. Errors
315	
316	The implementation should distinguish these user-visible failure categories:
317	
318	### Invalid skill name
319	
320	The requested name violates the naming rules.
321	
322	### Skill not found
323	
324	No matching skill directory exists.
325	
326	The error should list the roots searched.
327	
328	### Invalid skill directory
329	
330	The first matching path is not a readable directory or does not contain a
331	readable `SKILL.md`.
332	
333	### Invalid skill metadata
334	
335	Frontmatter is malformed, required fields are missing, or `name` does not match
336	the directory.
337	
338	### Unsupported skill API
339	
340	The skill declares an unsupported `skill_api`.
341	
342	Error messages should include:
343	
344	- the requested skill name;
345	- the relevant path;
346	- the reason for failure;
347	- a concise corrective action.
348	
349	A large hierarchy of resolver-specific exception classes is not required.
350	These categories may be represented by a small error type with a reason code.
351	
352	---
353	
354	## 12. CLI support
355	
356	The initial implementation should expose three commands.
357	
358	### 12.1 List skills
359	
360	```bash
361	wakil skills list
362	```
363	
364	Shows the effective skill names and selected source:
365	
366	```text
367	article-ingestion     user
368	entity-resolution     builtin
369	meeting-synthesis     kb-local
370	```
371	
372	The command scans all roots and applies normal precedence.
373	
374	### 12.2 Show resolution
375	
376	```bash
377	wakil skills which meeting-synthesis
378	```
379	
380	Shows the selected path:
381	
382	```text
383	/Users/example/my-kb/skills/meeting-synthesis/SKILL.md
384	```
385	
386	A verbose form may also show the ordered roots and any shadowed matches:
387	
388	```bash
389	wakil skills which meeting-synthesis --verbose
390	```
391	
392	### 12.3 Validate skills
393	
394	```bash
395	wakil skills validate
396	wakil skills validate meeting-synthesis
397	```
398	
399	Validation checks:
400	
401	- root accessibility;
402	- skill directory naming;
403	- presence and readability of `SKILL.md`;
404	- frontmatter parsing;
405	- metadata-name agreement;
406	- supported `skill_api`.
407	
408	Commands for copying, diffing, resetting, or rebasing skills are useful
409	conveniences but are outside the initial resolver scope. Ordinary filesystem
410	tools are sufficient until those workflows prove cumbersome.
411	
412	---
413	
414	## 13. Upgrade behavior
415	
416	Application upgrades may add, remove, or update built-in skills.
417	
418	Upgrades must never:
419	
420	- modify knowledge-base-local skills;
421	- modify user-level skills;
422	- merge built-in changes into overrides;
423	- delete overrides.
424	
425	A local override continues to take precedence after an upgrade.
426	
427	The initial implementation does not need to determine whether an override is
428	stale. Users can compare local and built-in files with standard diff tools or a
429	future convenience command.
430	
431	---
432	
433	## 14. Security boundary
434	
435	Skills are trusted local content owned by the single user.
436	
437	The resolver must still:
438	
439	- validate names before constructing paths;
440	- prevent path traversal through skill names;
441	- avoid executing code during discovery or validation;
442	- load supporting files only from the selected skill directory.
443	
444	Any future support for executable scripts requires a separate execution and
445	permission design.
446	
447	---
448	
449	## 15. Core algorithm
450	
451	```python
452	def resolve_skill(name: str, context: ResolutionContext) -> ResolvedSkill:
453	    validate_skill_name(name)
454	
455	    roots = normalize_roots([
456	        *parse_skill_path(context.environment),
457	        context.kb_root / "skills",
458	        context.user_skill_root,
459	        context.builtin_skill_root,
460	    ])
461	
462	    for root in roots:
463	        skill_dir = root.path / name
464	
465	        if not skill_dir.exists():
466	            continue
467	
468	        skill = load_and_validate_skill(skill_dir, expected_name=name)
469	
470	        return ResolvedSkill(
471	            name=name,
472	            source=root.source,
473	            root=root.path,
474	            directory=skill_dir,
475	            manifest=skill.manifest,
476	            metadata=skill.metadata,
477	        )
478	
479	    raise SkillNotFound(name=name, searched_roots=roots)
480	```
481	
482	`load_and_validate_skill` must fail if the selected directory or `SKILL.md` is
483	invalid. It must not continue searching lower-precedence roots.
484	
485	---
486	
487	## 16. Required tests
488	
489	The initial test suite should cover:
490	
491	### Resolution
492	
493	- built-in skill resolves when no override exists;
494	- user-level skill overrides built-in;
495	- KB-local skill overrides user-level and built-in;
496	- `WAKIL_SKILL_PATH` overrides default roots;
497	- first matching implementation is selected.
498	
499	### Invalid overrides
500	
501	- missing `SKILL.md` blocks fallback;
502	- malformed frontmatter blocks fallback;
503	- mismatched metadata name blocks fallback;
504	- unsupported `skill_api` blocks fallback;
505	- unreadable selected skill blocks fallback.
506	
507	### Path handling
508	
509	- missing default roots are ignored;
510	- duplicate roots are removed;
511	- `~` and environment variables expand;
512	- empty path-list entries are ignored;
513	- invalid skill names are rejected;
514	- relative supporting files resolve within the selected directory.
515	
516	### CLI diagnostics
517	
518	- `skills list` reports the effective source;
519	- `skills which` reports the selected path;
520	- `skills validate` identifies invalid roots and skills.
521	
522	---
523	
524	## 17. Deferred capabilities
525	
526	The following should be considered only after real usage demonstrates a need:
527	
528	- configuration-defined roots in addition to `WAKIL_SKILL_PATH`;
529	- explicit per-invocation skill-directory overrides;
530	- skill copy, diff, and reset commands;
531	- content digests and provenance metadata;
532	- stale-override detection;
533	- dependency declarations;
534	- aliases;
535	- live reload and cache invalidation;
536	- protected skill names;
537	- script execution.
538	
539	Deferring these keeps the resolver small and avoids committing to behavior that
540	may never be needed.
541	
542	---
543	
544	## 18. Invariants
545	
546	The implementation must preserve these rules:
547	
548	1. Skill roots have a deterministic order.
549	2. The first matching skill directory wins.
550	3. An invalid winning skill blocks fallback.
551	4. A skill and all of its resources come from one directory.
552	5. Built-in skills are the final fallback.
553	6. Local skills are never modified by application upgrades.
554	7. The selected source is inspectable.
555	8. Discovery and validation do not execute skill-provided code.
556	
557	These invariants define the essential skill-resolution contract.

1	# Skill refactor
2	
3	Build a catalog of extensible skills useful for managing ingest and maintenance of a knowledge base in markdown format.
4	
5	## Goal
6	
7	I have a set of skills (housed at `~/Projects/kb`) that works overall pretty well for ingesting raw sources, doing interpreted synthesis of them into usable content, and enriched through linkages with existing entities in the KB.
8	
9	However, that set of skills has diverged and evolved to a point where it contradicts itself and can fail silently.  It is also intimately connected to the `gbrain` tool, and which I want to move away from.  This is the fundamental motivation for switching to create `wakil`.
10	
11	I'd like to take that set of skills and transform them into a set of skills for `wakil` that retains the deep expertise already built in there, while fixing issues of rot, duplication, contradiction, and coupling with legacy tools (e.g. `gbrain`).
12	
13	The existing system also provides core functionality that gets consistently overridden as Hermes (my agent orchestrator) evolves skills by updating these skills in-place. This is a key source of the rot I'm experiencing.
14	
15	I'd like to introduce in `wakil` a core set of "golden" skills and best practices that can be overridden by a user or by hermes.
16	
17	---
18	
19	## Core skills
20	
21	This is the set of core skills that the `wakil` kb should support.  The key functionality should be captured from `~/Projects/kb/.hermes/skills`, after refactoring and fixing of the issues outlined below and then routed into one (or more) of the skills outlined below.  The Hermes skills contain a lot of useful nuance after having evolved and this should not be lost, just normalized and abstracted away from `gbrain`.
22	
23	1. `ingest-source` — Coordinates the complete workflow for bringing external material into the knowledge base.
24	2. `source-ingestion` — Retrieves and normalizes raw source content and its provenance.
25	3. `content-synthesis` — Produces a standalone interpretive note from source material.
26	4. `entity-resolution` — Matches referenced people, companies, projects, and concepts to existing entities.
27	5. `entity-enrichment` — Adds meaningful entity links and creates missing entities where appropriate.
28	6. `note-routing` — Determines the correct note type, filename, and location using `RESOLVER.md`.
29	7. `note-conformance` — Applies and validates note structure and metadata using `SCHEMA.md`.
30	8. `knowledge-query` — Answers questions by translating them into effective QMD retrievals.
31	9. `knowledge-research` — Investigates a question across the KB and external sources with traceable evidence.
32	10. `note-revision` — Incorporates new information into existing notes without discarding useful prior knowledge.
33	11. `skill-authoring` — Creates, overrides, and validates skills without modifying built-in versions.
34	12. `kb-commit` — Reviews and commits KB changes using repository-specific validation and summaries.
35	
36	### 1. `ingest-source`
37	
38	`ingest-source` is the user-facing workflow for bringing external material into the knowledge base.
39	
40	Responsibilities:
41	
42	- coordinate source retrieval, synthesis, entity integration, routing, and conformance;
43	- select the appropriate ingestion behavior for the source type;
44	- preserve progress and surface failures at the stage where they occur;
45	- produce both a normalized source note and a synthesized knowledge note where appropriate.
46	
47	`ingest-source` should orchestrate the underlying skills rather than duplicate their implementation.
48	
49	A typical workflow is:
50	
51	```text
52	source-ingestion
53	→ content-synthesis
54	→ entity-resolution
55	→ entity-enrichment
56	→ note-routing
57	→ note-conformance
58	→ persist notes
59	```
60	
61	---
62	
63	### 2. `source-ingestion`
64	
65	`source-ingestion` retrieves or accepts external material and stores it in a normalized source-note format.
66	
67	Responsibilities:
68	
69	- identify the source type;
70	- retrieve or accept the raw content;
71	- preserve source metadata and provenance;
72	- normalize the content into a common source-note structure;
73	- hand the normalized source to `content-synthesis`.
74	
75	Supported source types may include:
76	
77	- meeting transcripts;
78	- web articles;
79	- reader applications such as Readwise;
80	- Kindle books and highlights;
81	- YouTube videos;
82	- Twitter/X posts and threads.
83	
84	Source-specific implementations may later sit beneath this skill:
85	
86	```text
87	article-ingestion
88	meeting-transcript-ingestion
89	youtube-ingestion
90	kindle-ingestion
91	readwise-ingestion
92	social-post-ingestion
93	```
94	
95	The initial implementation should introduce specialized skills only where source handling differs enough to justify them.
96	
97	---
98	
99	### 3. `content-synthesis`
100	
101	`content-synthesis` turns source material into a coherent standalone knowledge note.
102	
103	Responsibilities:
104	
105	- identify central themes, claims, conclusions, and implications;
106	- distinguish source statements from inferred conclusions;
107	- produce a readable note that does not require reopening the raw source;
108	- preserve traceability to the source material;
109	- extract decisions, questions, actions, insights, or arguments as appropriate;
110	- avoid reducing the output to a transcript summary or list of excerpts.
111	
112	The same source may be synthesized differently depending on its purpose. A meeting transcript, for example, may produce a meeting record, decision note, project update, or reusable concept note.
113	
114	The name `content-synthesis` is preferable to `source-synthesis` because the skill may later synthesize across multiple sources or existing notes.
115	
116	---
117	
118	### 4. `entity-resolution`
119	
120	`entity-resolution` determines whether a referenced entity corresponds to an existing knowledge-base entity.

483	- Allow users to override built-in skills without modifying system-managed files.
484	- Resolve skills deterministically from ordered local, user, and built-in sources, without merging implementations.
485	- Keep resolution transparent, validated, and resilient to upgrades and stale overrides.
486	
487	The skill resolution system lets users customize built-in behavior by placing replacement skills in higher-precedence local directories, while preserving bundled skills as reliable fallbacks. It resolves each skill deterministically from an ordered set of sources, selects one complete skill directory without merging files across implementations, validates the chosen skill before use, and makes the active source easy to inspect. Let me lay out what I found, then ask you a few questions to pin down the integration design.

**What the code/docs actually say (not aspirational — this is current state):**

1. **Skill overrides are whole-directory shadowing, not diffing/layering.** `docs/skill-resolution-specification.md` §3 explicitly lists "inheritance or partial file-level overrides," "merging files across skill directories," and "automatic drift detection or merging" as *non-goals*. Resolution order is `WAKIL_SKILL_PATH` → `<kb-root>/skills` → `~/.config/wakil/skills` → built-in, first match wins, full directory replaces the built-in one. There's no `wakil skills diff` — §12.3 says that's deliberately deferred ("ordinary filesystem tools are sufficient until proven cumbersome"). So your goal of "it's clear what Hermes has changed" isn't something wakil tracks for you today — you'd get that from `git diff` if the override lives somewhere version-controlled (e.g. kb-local `skills/`), not from wakil itself.

2. **"Hermes" is already named in `docs/skill-refactor.md`** as your existing agent orchestrator that previously owned `~/Projects/kb/.hermes/skills` and drove the KB via a legacy `gbrain` MCP server. The doc states plainly: *"The existing system also provides core functionality that gets consistently overridden as Hermes evolves skills by updating these skills in-place. This is a key source of the rot I'm experiencing."* `wakil`'s whole golden-skill + resolver design exists specifically to stop that in-place mutation. That's useful — it means this isn't a new integration to design from scratch, it's the stated purpose of the project.

3. **The resolver is built but not yet load-bearing.** `src/wakil/skills/resolver.py` implements the full precedence/override logic and is exposed via `wakil skills list|which|validate`, but wakil's actual skill *execution* (`src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`) still calls an older `wakil.llm.skill_loader.load_skill()` that only reads the flat legacy `src/wakil/skills/` directory and has **no awareness of overrides at all**. # Wakil ↔ Hermes integration: architecture guidance (no code changes)

## Context

The user runs Hermes (Nous Research's agent CLI — model-routing agent with its
own MCP client, `SOUL.md` identity, `MEMORY.md`/`USER.md` persistent memory,
and a skills layer compatible with the `agentskills.io` open standard) as
their day-to-day interactive agent against a personal Markdown knowledge base.
`wakil` (this repo) is being built to replace the legacy `gbrain` MCP tool as
the deterministic substrate underneath that KB — see `docs/skill-refactor.md`:
Hermes previously owned `~/Projects/kb/.hermes/skills` and mutated them
in-place as it evolved, which is named directly as "a key source of the rot"
motivating `wakil`'s golden-skill-catalog-plus-resolver design.

The user's open question was less "how do I write code" and more "am I
modeling this integration correctly" — hence guidance/correction, not
implementation. Another agent is actively mid-refactor on branch
`feat/skill-catalog` (uncommitted edits under `src/wakil/skills/builtin/`),
so this session deliberately does not touch skill code.

## What's actually true today (corrections to the starting mental model)

1. **Overrides are whole-directory shadowing, not diffing/layering.**
   `docs/skill-resolution-specification.md` §3 lists partial/file-level
   overrides, cross-directory merging, and drift detection as explicit
   non-goals. Resolution order is `WAKIL_SKILL_PATH` → `<kb-root>/skills` →
   `~/.config/wakil/skills` → built-in; first match wins; a full directory
   replaces the built-in one. There is no `wakil skills diff` — §12.3 defers
   that ("ordinary filesystem tools are sufficient until proven cumbersome").
   **"Clear what Hermes changed" comes from `git diff` on a version-controlled
   override directory, not from anything wakil computes.** This is exactly
   why kb-local `skills/` (git-native, travels with the vault) is the right
   choice — see Decision 2 below.

2. **The resolver is real but not yet load-bearing.** `src/wakil/skills/resolver.py`
   implements the full precedence/override/validation logic and is exposed via
   `wakil skills list|which|validate`. But actual skill *execution* —
   `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py` → `wakil.llm.skill_loader.load_skill()` —
   still reads only the flat legacy `src/wakil/skills/` directory and has no
   awareness of overrides at all (its own docstring says extension happens "by
   forking and editing them, not by runtime discovery," directly contradicting
   the resolver spec). **Consequence: right now, a kb-local override under
   `<kb-root>/skills/<name>/` is inspectable (`wakil skills which <name>`
   will correctly report it as selected) but has no effect on `wakil ingest`/
   `wakil enrich` behavior until the other agent's `feat/skill-catalog` work
   wires the resolver into `ingest_service.py`.** Check on that branch before
   relying on kb-local overrides actually changing wakil's behavior.

3. **No MCP server or external API exists in wakil.** The only integration
   surface today is the `wakil` CLI itself (subprocess). Hermes does have
   native MCP client support, which is a real option for later if the "Hermes
   shouldn't need to know about wakil" boundary ever gets renegotiated — noted
   here for the record, not recommended now (see Decision 1).

4. **Wakil's ambition is broader than skills** — this shapes what "Hermes
   uses wakil" should mean day to day (`PROMPT.md` §Memory Model, §Dream
   Function; `README.md` §Memory lifecycle):
   - **Memory lifecycle**: ingested sources propose `candidate` memories;
     `working → candidate → durable`/`rejected`, `durable → archived`, with
     retrieval fading by state/recency/confidence. Implemented and CLI-exposed
     (`wakil memory list/show/promote/reject/archive`).
   - **Dream**: a deeper, non-literal synthesis pass over the KB — recurring
     themes, weak/surprising relationships, proposed links and concept notes,
     a human-reviewable report, never auto-applied. This is entirely
     unimplemented (`TODO.md` Phase 6, all boxes unchecked) — no `wakil dream`
     command exists yet.
   - Both are **wakil-owned, KB-domain memory** (facts/events/relationships
     extracted from ingested material) — a different thing from Hermes's own
     `MEMORY.md`/`USER.md` (Hermes's *operational* memory about the user and
     session continuity). These two memory systems should stay separate:
     wakil's memory table is knowledge-base content, not agent self-knowledge,
     and nothing here suggests syncing them.

## Decisions made (from clarifying questions)

1. **Invocation model: CLI subprocess, loosely coupled.** Hermes shells out to
   `wakil` commands (`ingest`, `search`, `query`, `memory`, `git`, and later
   `dream`) exactly as it previously called `gbrain`'s MCP tools. Neither
   system needs to know about the other's internals — wakil doesn't gain
   Hermes-specific code, and Hermes doesn't need to parse wakil's skill
   catalog to function. This preserves wakil's local-first, single-purpose
   CLI shape (`CLAUDE.md` engineering principle: don't add complexity without
   clear, self-evident use-case impact) and avoids resurrecting the tight
   coupling that caused the original rot.

2. **Override location: kb-local `<kb-root>/skills/`.** When Hermes (or the
   user) needs to customize a wakil "golden" skill for a specific vault, the
   override goes in `<kb-root>/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`, committed to
   the KB's own git history. This is the only override tier that's naturally
   git-diffable per-vault and reviewable alongside the notes it affects,
   matching the project's git-native/human-review design bias. It also
   out-ranks `~/.config/wakil/skills` and built-in in the resolver, so it's
   the correct tier for "this vault's Hermes has opinions that differ from
   wakil's defaults."

3. **Session scope: guidance only.** No code changes this session. The
   resolver-to-execution wiring gap (point 2 above) is being worked on
   concurrently on `feat/skill-catalog` — pick that up as a follow-up once
   that branch lands, rather than duplicating it here.

## Recommended follow-ups (not done in this session)

- **Verify the wiring gap is closed** before relying on kb-local overrides in
  practice: once `feat/skill-catalog` merges, confirm `ingest_service.py`
  resolves skills through `src/wakil/skills/resolver.py` rather than the
  legacy `wakil.llm.skill_loader.load_skill()` (`skill_loader.py`'s current
  docstring is the tell that it hasn't happened yet).
- **`wakil dream` is unbuilt** (`PROMPT.md` §Dream Function, `TODO.md` Phase
  6) but is core to the product's ambition — worth prioritizing once the
  skill-catalog refactor settles, since "propose connections/links/notes,
  human-reviewed, never auto-applied" is exactly the kind of synthesis a
  Hermes session would want to trigger and read a report from.
- **Format-compatibility check, optional/low-cost**: Hermes's skills layer is
  documented as compatible with the `agentskills.io` open standard; wakil's
  `SKILL.md` frontmatter is documented as "Claude-Skills-compatible." Worth a
  quick check (not now) of whether these are close enough that Hermes could
  point its own skill loader at the same `<kb-root>/skills` directory as a
  convenience — this would be pure filesystem convention, not a code
  integration, so it doesn't violate Decision 1's loose-coupling boundary if
  it ever becomes useful.

## Verification

No code changed. To confirm the current (pre-wiring-fix) state described
above still holds before acting on it: `uv run wakil -w <kb> skills which
<name> -v` shows resolution/precedence correctly today; cross-check against
`ingest_service.py`'s actual skill-loading call to confirm whether the
resolver wiring has landed yet.

## Operating model: how a user or Hermes should manage a KB via wakil

With the resolver wired in, the full loop is now real, not aspirational:

```text
wakil init <kb>                          # one-time: SQLite index, git detection, QMD check
wakil ingest transcript|article|text ...  # deterministic capture -> sources/
wakil enrich <source-id>                  # model-assisted: content-synthesis +
                                           #   entity-resolution, using resolved skills,
                                           #   preview before write
wakil memory list/promote/reject/archive  # human curation of extracted candidates
wakil search / wakil query                # QMD + FTS5 + memory, cited answers
wakil git summary / history               # audit what wakil changed and when
wakil skills list/which/validate/lint     # inspect what's active and why
wakil dream ...                           # (unbuilt, see below) periodic synthesis pass
```

The division of labor that matches the "loosely coupled" decision above:
**wakil owns the deterministic, auditable, git-backed KB operations and the
judgment prose for its own fixed pipeline steps (content-synthesis,
entity-resolution, note-routing, etc.); Hermes owns the interactive judgment
about *when* to call which wakil subcommand and what to do with the output**
(approve a preview, promote a memory, act on a dream report). Hermes should
treat `wakil` as an ordinary CLI tool in its toolset — same shape as any other
subprocess-based tool — with no special-cased protocol.

Customizing wakil's behavior per-vault now works end-to-end:

1. `wakil skills which content-synthesis -v` — see the currently selected
   source (built-in, user-level, or kb-local) and the full search order.
2. Drop a replacement at `<kb-root>/skills/content-synthesis/SKILL.md`,
   commit it to the KB's own git history.
3. `wakil skills which content-synthesis -v` again — confirms kb-local now
   wins; `wakil skills validate` catches a broken override before it silently
   blocks fallback (invalid overrides don't fall through to built-in, by
   design — spec §9.2).
4. `git log`/`git diff` on that file, inside the KB's own repo, is the answer
   to "what has Hermes (or I) changed" — wakil deliberately doesn't compute
   this itself (see point 1 above), but because the override lives in the
   KB's git history, the KB's own git tooling already gives you exactly that.

This is the concrete mechanism behind Decision 2: kb-local overrides are the
right tier precisely because they're the only tier that's naturally
git-diffable per-vault, and that diffability is now backed by a resolver that
actually affects execution.

## Recommended follow-ups (not done in this session)

- **`wakil dream` is unbuilt**

# ingest-source

This is the top-level, user-facing workflow. It does not do its own content
judgment — it decides which of the six focused skills below apply to the
material in front of it, in what order, and gets out of the way once each
has done its job. If you catch yourself deciding what a note should say,
which entity a mention resolves to, or where a file belongs, stop — that
judgment belongs to `content-synthesis`, `entity-resolution`, or
`note-routing` respectively, not to this skill.

## The two-command backbone

For the three shapes `wakil` ingests natively, the whole pipeline is two
commands:

=== source-ingestion ===
---
name: source-ingestion
description: Normalize non-native source material (meeting exports, PDFs, voice notes, YouTube videos, scanned documents) into wakil's three CLI-native shapes — transcript, text, or article — with a rich --context string, before handing off to `wakil ingest`. Use whenever raw material doesn't already fit one of those three shapes as-is.
skill_api: 1
---

# source-ingestion

`wakil ingest` only knows three shapes of input: a transcript file, a plain
text file, and a web article URL. Most of what actually shows up — a PDF
email export, a voice memo, a YouTube link, a scanned document, a folder of
mixed files — is none of these until someone makes it one. That's this
skill's whole job: turn whatever raw material arrived into one of the three
CLI-native shapes, with a `--context` string rich enough that the model
steps downstream don't have to guess, and then get out of the way.

This is deliberately upstream of judgment about what the material *means*.
Don't extract claims, don't decide what's worth a note, don't resolve
entities here — that's the ingestion DAG's job once your normalized file
reaches it.

=== knowledge-query ===
---
name: knowledge-query
description: Decides which retrieval mode to reach for (wakil search/query, mode search|vsearch|query), how to weigh and cite the results, and when recency should outrank compiled truth; use whenever a question needs to be answered from the knowledge base rather than from general knowledge.

# knowledge-query

You are the retrieval-and-answer step. A question has come in that should be
answered from the knowledge base — "what do we know about X", "who is Y",
"catch me up on Z", "did the source say anything about W". Your job is not
how QMD or SQLite FTS rank results internally; that's `wakil search` /
`wakil query`'s problem, and it's already solved. Your job is: which mode to
invoke, how much of the result set to actually read, how to weigh it against
what else the knowledge base already says, and how to present an answer that
never overstates what was retrieved.

## Brain-first lookup

Search the knowledge base before reaching for any external tool. `wakil

=== knowledge-research ===
---
name: knowledge-research
description: Investigate a question or claim using the knowledge base and, where the KB comes up thin, external sources — with traceable citations and an explicit fact/inference/gap split. Use when knowledge-query's brain-first lookup is genuinely insufficient, or when a specific claim needs to be checked rather than just looked up.
skill_api: 1

# knowledge-research

You are the investigation step. `knowledge-query` answers a question using
material already present in the knowledge base; you exist for what's left
over — a question the KB only partially covers, a claim that needs checking
rather than retrieving, or a topic where the useful answer requires evidence
the KB doesn't have yet. Keep the boundary explicit:

knowledge-research → investigates a question using the KB and, where necessary,

=== skill-authoring ===
---
name: skill-authoring
description: Author, edit, override, or promote a SKILL.md file within wakil's skill catalog — MECE scope-check, frontmatter contract, and override/promotion mechanics. Use when creating a new skill, extending an existing one, overriding a built-in, or porting a kb-local skill into the shipped catalog.
skill_api: 1
---

# skill-authoring

This is the meta-skill: it governs how every other `SKILL.md` in this catalog
— and this file itself — gets written, edited, overridden, or retired. It does
not decide what a *note* should say (`content-synthesis`, `note-revision`) or
where a note belongs (`note-routing`); it decides how a *skill file* is
scoped, shaped, and placed. Use it whenever asked to create a skill, extend
one, override a built-in without touching the shipped copy, or lift a
kb-local skill into the shipped catalog.

## When to use

- Asked to add a new skill, or to encode a new repeatable procedure.
- Asked to fix, extend, or correct an existing skill, built-in or override.

=== kb-commit ===
---
name: kb-commit
description: Commit pending changes in a wakil-managed knowledge base with wakil's kind-prefixed message convention, grouped into reviewable logical change sets. Use after manual edits, after note-revision, or after a schema migrate run that wasn't committed inline.
skill_api: 1
---

# kb-commit

This skill governs commits to a **knowledge-base workspace** wakil manages — not
commits to wakil's own source code. It is a different convention from whatever
governs this dev repo's own history; do not blend the two.

`wakil ingest`, `wakil enrich`, and `wakil schema migrate` each have their own
`--branch`/`--commit` flags and already commit their own output correctly when
those flags are passed. This skill exists for what those flags don't cover:
manual edits to a note, output from a `note-revision` pass, or a
`schema migrate` run made without `--commit`. If a wakil command's own commit
flag is available and appropriate for the change at hand, prefer it over this
skill — this is the fallback path, not the default one.

That's the real answer, and it's already built into the repo: `resolve_skill`/`load_skill` is only ever called from two places — `wakil enrich`'s internal DAG (`article`/`text`/`transcript`/`entity-resolve`, four narrowly-scoped skills) and the `wakil skills` diagnostic commands. The other 12 "golden catalog" skills — `ingest-source`, `source-ingestion`, `knowledge-query`, `knowledge-research`, `kb-commit`, `content-synthesis`, `entity-resolution`, `entity-enrichment`, `note-routing`, `note-conformance`, `note-revision`, `skill-authoring` — are **never loaded by wakil's own code at all**. I checked their prose, and they're written in second-person imperative voice, directly addressed to an operating agent:

- `ingest-source`: *"This is the top-level, user-facing workflow... For the three shapes wakil ingests natively, the whole pipeline is two commands"* — literally spells out `wakil ingest` → `wakil enrich`.
- `knowledge-query`: *"Search the knowledge base before reaching for any external tool. wakil search/query..."*
- `kb-commit`: *"wakil ingest, wakil enrich, and wakil schema migrate already commit their own output... prefer it over this skill"* — even tells the caller when *not* to use it.
- `content-synthesis`: explicitly scoped to work *"outside `wakil enrich`'s DAG"* — i.e., for manual synthesis Hermes does itself, distinct from the internal skill wakil's own code uses.

So this catalog isn't wakil's internal prompt library with some extra unused files — it's an already-written runbook for exactly the kind of agent Hermes is, sitting in wakil's repo in Claude-Skills-compatible format, currently orphaned (nothing loads it).

**Recommendation:** point Hermes's own skill loader at wakil's resolved `skills/` directory (or a curated subset — the 12 golden ones, not the 4 internal ones) so Hermes reads these as its own skills, rather than writing a separate AGENTS.md/.hermes.md runbook that would just re-describe the same CLI surface and drift from it over time. The tradeoff: this only works cleanly if Hermes's skill-directory discovery is filesystem-configurable per-project — I only fetched Hermes's features overview page, not its skills-specific docs, so I haven't confirmed how it points at a project's skill directory. Want me to check that page next, or are you set on this direction already?

4	description: |
5	  Ingest meeting transcripts into brain pages with attendee enrichment, entity
6	  propagation, and timeline merge. A meeting is NOT fully ingested until the
7	  enrich skill has processed every entity.
8	triggers:
9	  - "meeting transcript"

26	---
27	
28	# Meeting Ingestion Skill
29	
30	> **Filing rule:** Read `skills/_brain-filing-rules.md` before creating any new page.
31	
32	## Contract
33	
34	This skill guarantees:
35	- Meeting page created with attendees, summary, key decisions, action items
36	- EVERY attendee gets a people page (created or updated)
37	- EVERY company discussed gets entity propagation
38	- Timeline entries on ALL mentioned entities (timeline merge)
39	- Meeting is NOT fully ingested until enrich runs for every entity
40	- Back-links created bidirectionally
41	- If a **prep doc** exists for the meeting, the meeting page reconciles it (which
42	  prepped questions/topics were answered, which threads are still open, brief
43	  analysis) and the prep ↔ meeting pages are cross-linked bidirectionally (see
44	  Phase 2.5)
45	
46	> **Convention:** See `skills/conventions/quality.md` for Iron Law back-linking.
47	
48	Every attendee and company mentioned MUST get a back-link from their page to
49	the meeting page. An unlinked mention is a broken brain.
50	
51	## Phases
52	
53	### Phase 0: Discover the transcript(s)
54	
55	When the user says "ingest the transcripts I added" (or any variation that implies one or more new transcript files are sitting on disk), do NOT ask where they are. Find them yourself:
56	
57	1. Ingest audio transcripts: check `./sources/audio/` for `.whisper`  or other audio files. If a found audio file is a `.whisper` file, use `unzip -p <file> metadata.json` to extract the JSON transcript and metadata.
58	2. `git -C /Users/ebridges/Projects/kb log --oneline sources/transcripts/<file>` on any tracked-but-unfamiliar file — a single recent commit confirms it's new this session.
59	3. If the user named a specific topic ("the Lyon Szot call"), still run the git-status check first — the file may already be committed as a stub from a prior turn and the user has now filled it in (see the resynth-after-stub rule).
60	4. Confirm filename → date → topic by reading the first ~30 lines of each candidate before assuming.
61	
62	Asking "where is the transcript?" when `git status` would have shown it is friction the user shouldn't absorb — same principle as the email-retrieval rule below.
63	
64	### Phase 1: Parse the transcript
65	
66	Extract from the transcript:
67	- Attendees (names, roles if available)
68	- Date, time, duration
69	- Key topics discussed
70	- Decisions made
71	- Action items with owners
72	- Companies and projects mentioned
73	
74	**Date precedence:** filenames and source frontmatter can be capture dates, not meeting dates. If email/calendar context proves the actual meeting date differs from the transcript filename, use the event date for the meeting page and cite the filename/source page separately.
75	
76	**Verify company/entity spelling against an external source before slugging.** Apple Notes / Fathom / hand-typed transcript filenames frequently contain typos in proper nouns. Before creating `companies/<slug>` or `people/<slug>`, cross-check the name against (a) the recruiter's email (use the `references/email-retrieval.md` pattern), (b) the company website, or (c) a LinkedIn / press-release URL passed by a recruiter. If the filename and the authoritative source disagree, **rename the source file to match the authoritative spelling** before slugging entities — don't propagate the typo into the brain.
77	
78	**Transcript stub case (header-only, no body):** Some transcripts are created as stubs. Treat this as a valid case, not an error.
79	**Verification of write:** ALWAYS verify that files were successfully written to disk (e.g., via `search_files` or `read_file`) after a `write_file` call. Do not assume a successful `execute_code` output means the file system was actually updated.
80	**File extensions:** Ensure all brain pages are written with the `.md` extension. Missing extensions will result in files that are invisible to brain search and link resolution.
81	- Still create the meeting page; mark the source as "no transcript was captured" in the body.
82	- Reconstruct meaning from adjacent sources — the related email thread (use `references/email-retrieval.md`), the user's later summary in chat, calendar invites, follow-up messages. Cite those sources explicitly.
83	- Frontmatter `source:` should be `notes` (not `transcript`) so downstream tools don't expect a chunk-embeddable body.
84	- **The stub can become a full transcript mid-session or in a follow-up session.** If the user says "I added the transcript" (or anything similar), re-read the source file from disk before assuming yesterday's stub is still a stub. When a populated transcript appears, rewrite the meeting page and re-synthesize the Compiled Truth on every entity page that references the meeting — do not trust the stub-era summary to still be accurate. Commit the rewrite as `🧠 synth(<entity>)` so the diff is legible as a knowledge upgrade, not a typo fix.
85	
86	**When the user references their own email/message, retrieve it before asking them to paste content.** See `references/email-retrieval.md` for the gog gmail pattern. Asking "what did the email say?" when you can pull it yourself is friction the user shouldn't have to absorb.
87	
88	**Re-read source transcripts between turns when the user says "I added the transcript" or similar.** A source file you committed in a prior turn as a stub / header-only / partial capture may have been filled in by the user mid-thread. Do not rely on cached knowledge from your earlier `read_file` call. Sequence:
89	1. Re-read the source file on disk.
90	2. If substantive new content is present, rebuild the meeting page, the Sahil/Yuri/etc. people pages, and the company Compiled Truth from the now-complete source.
91	3. Commit the rebuild as a `🧠 synth(<entity>)` commit per the kb-commit skill — not `update` or `log`.
92	4. Run `gbrain check-backlinks fix --dir .` after the resynth; commit any incidental hygiene edits as a separate `🔗 link` commit (see Phase 7).
93	
94	**Sanity-check numeric claims against unit conventions; flag discrepancies in the brain page rather than silently propagating.** Recruiters and founders frequently misstate equity (basis points vs percent), comp ranges, valuations, and team headcounts in conversational settings. Common shapes:
95	- "45 basis points = 4.5% of the company" — wrong; 45 bps = 0.45%. (100 bps = 1%.)
96	- "$25M Series A" cited as the round size when public sources say $17M seed — note the discrepancy.
97	- "Hired 1,000 candidates" almost certainly means "interviewed/filtered" — capture the actual claim and the likely meaning separately.
98	When you spot one, write the verbatim claim **and** the corrected/queried value in the Compiled Truth or the meeting page, with explicit instruction-to-self language like "verify in writing before any deeper commitment." Never silently normalize the number — the discrepancy itself is signal about either the speaker's care with numbers or the agent's listening accuracy.
99	
100	**Preserve verbatim language for any exchange the user later acts on.** When a meeting drives a downstream user decision (decline, accept, escalate, negotiate, follow up), the meeting page MUST capture the exact words of the decisive exchange — not a paraphrase. Examples: the role-shape question and the founder's response that drove a decline; the comp number stated; the explicit deal-breaker raised. Paraphrasing the moment that drove the user's action loses the evidence needed for any later second-guessing or follow-up conversation. Quote it.
101	
102	**When a transcript presents multiple options before resolving on one, locate the resolution before you synthesize.** Conversational transcripts typically run: Option A described → Option B described → discussion → resolution. The agent's failure mode is to anchor on the first or most-elaborated option (often Option A, because the speaker explained it first and in most detail) and miss the resolution that picked Option B. Before writing the meeting page:
103	1. Identify every option presented. Note the line numbers.
104	2. Find the resolution — usually phrased as "in that vein, I think we'd be okay with X", "let's go with Y", "I'd rather do Z", or a direct answer to a "so which one?" question. If you can't find an explicit resolution, the meeting did NOT resolve it — flag as open, do not invent a resolution.
105	3. Watch for joint-pronoun language as a structural signal. "We hold them responsible" / "you, me, we" / "between us" implies BOTH parties are in the accountability chain. If you wrote a one-party-holds-everything structure, re-read those passages.
106	4. After drafting the meeting page, before propagating to entity pages, re-read the decision-relevant passage of the transcript one more time against your draft. Specifically check the financial/contractual terms (markups, fees, who-invoices-whom, who-holds-the-contract). These are the bits the user is most likely to correct because they care about them most.
107	5. When the user corrects a misread fact, do NOT just patch the most-recent page. Propagate the fix across every page that references the fact (meeting + project + company + person), in a single pass, in one ✏️ fix commit. Use `search_files` with the wrong-fact pattern to find all stale references before staging.
108	
109	### Phase 2: Create meeting page
110	
111	```markdown
112	# {Meeting Title} — {Date}
113	
114	**Attendees:** {list with links to people pages}
115	**Date:** {YYYY-MM-DD}
116	**Duration:** {if available}
117	
118	## Summary
119	{3-5 bullet key outcomes}
120	
121	## Key Decisions
122	{Decisions with context}
123	
124	## Action Items
125	{Tasks with owners and deadlines}
126	
127	## Prep Reconciliation
128	{ONLY when a prep doc exists — see Phase 2.5. Omit the section entirely otherwise.}
129	
130	## Discussion Notes
131	{Structured notes by topic}
132	```
133	
134	### Phase 2.5: Prep reconciliation (when a prep doc exists)
135	
136	Meetings the user prepped for produce a `*-prep.md` page (frontmatter `status:
137	prep`, usually same date-prefixed slug + `-prep`, same `company:`/attendees).
138	Closing that loop is where most of the durable value lands — an ingested meeting
139	that ignores its own prep throws away the "what did we set out to learn, and did
140	we?" analysis the user actually acts on.
141	
142	1. **Discover the prep doc.** Before writing the meeting page, look for a prep:
143	   - `search "{meeting topic} prep"` / brain query, AND
144	   - glob `meetings/**/{date}-*prep.md` and `meetings/**/*{entity}*prep.md`;
145	     check frontmatter for `status: prep` referencing the same company/attendees.
146	   - A prep may pre-date the meeting by days and use a slightly different slug
147	     (it was written before the final title) — match on date + entity, not exact
148	     slug. If none exists, skip this phase (omit the section); do not invent one.
149	2. **Read the prep's intent.** Pull out its planned questions, the topics/risks it
150	   flagged, the "landmines / do-nots," and any hypotheses about the room.
151	3. **Reconcile against the transcript.** In the meeting page's `## Prep
152	   Reconciliation` section, map:
153	   - **Asked & answered** — each prepped question that came up, with the answer.
154	   - **Answered without being asked** — prepped topics the counterparty
155	     volunteered.
156	   - **Landmines** — whether the do-nots were observed (note any that were hit).
157	   - **Still open / carry forward** — prepped threads the meeting did NOT resolve;
158	     these become follow-ups, and the highest-priority ones also belong in the
159	     user-facing action items (Output Format part 2).
160	   - **New — not in the prep read** — the sharpest surprises the meeting surfaced;
161	     label them explicitly as new so they aren't mistaken for confirmed prep.
162	   - Keep it brief and analytic, not a transcript re-dump. Cite each line per the
163	     quality convention.
164	4. **Cross-link bidirectionally.** Add a `**Prep:**` link on the meeting page to
165	   the prep doc, AND an `## Outcome` section on the prep doc linking forward to the
166	   meeting with a one-paragraph result (what happened, the key surprise, pointer
167	   to the reconciliation). A prep with no forward link to its outcome is a dead
168	   end.
169	
170	### Phase 3: Attendee enrichment (MANDATORY)
171	
172	For EACH attendee:
173	1. `gbrain search "{name}"` — does a people page exist?
174	2. If NO → create via enrich skill (this is mandatory, not optional) unless the attendee is the user/self and no self page convention exists; in that case use plain text (`Edward Bridges`) rather than inventing a self page solely for a backlink.
175	3. If YES → update compiled truth with meeting context
176	4. Add timeline entry on the person's page:
177	   `gbrain timeline-add <person-slug> <date> "Attended <meeting-title>"`
178	
179	**Note (v0.10.1):** Once the meeting page is written via `gbrain put`, the
180	auto-link post-hook automatically creates `attended` links from the meeting
181	to each attendee whose page is referenced as `[Name](people/slug)`. You don't
182	need to call `gbrain link` for attendees. You DO still need `gbrain timeline-add`
183	for dated events (auto-link only handles links, not timeline entries).
184	
185	### Phase 4: Entity propagation (MANDATORY)
186	
187	For each company, project, or concept discussed:
188	1. Check brain for existing page
189	2. Create/update as needed
190	3. Add timeline entry referencing the meeting
191	4. Back-link from entity page to meeting page
192	
193	### Phase 5: Timeline merge
194	
195	The same event appears on ALL mentioned entities' timelines. If Alice met Bob at
196	Acme Corp, the event goes on Alice's page, Bob's page, AND Acme Corp's page.
197	
198	### Phase 6: Sync
199	
200	`gbrain sync` to update the index.
201	
202	### Phase 7: Reciprocal back-link audit (optional but recommended)
203	
204	After sync, run `gbrain check-backlinks check` to see if any new pages
205	created in this session have unreciprocated mentions, then `gbrain
206	check-backlinks fix --dir .` to repair them.
207	
208	**Heads up:** `check-backlinks fix` can also touch pre-existing pages that
209	were missing reciprocal entries before this session (entity pages
210	referenced from other entity pages without back-links). Those incidental
211	hygiene edits are real fixes — keep them — but **commit them as a
212	separate `🔗 link(...)` commit**, not bundled with the session's content
213	commits. The `kb-commit` skill calls this out under "Evaluate Scope and
214	Suggest Splits."
215	
216	## Output Format
217	
218	Two-part output is mandatory when the meeting drives downstream user work:
219	
220	1. **Status line:** "Meeting ingested: {N} attendees enriched, {N} entities updated, {N} action items captured." Plus the commit hashes if commits were made.
221	2. **User-facing action items list.** This is NOT the same as the `## Action Items` section on the meeting page. The meeting page captures action items as they were stated in the call (e.g. "Joe: send updated Section 6 language"). The user-facing list synthesizes those into the user's next concrete moves in priority order — what to do this week, what to do next, what to track during execution. Format:
222	
223	   ```markdown
224	   ## Action Items for You
225	
226	   ### 🔴 This week — block the project on these
227	   1. Do X. Reasoning: ... Tone: ...
228	   2. Wait for Y from {counterparty}. What to look for in their response: ...
229	
230	   ### 🟡 Pre-{next milestone}
231	   3. ...
232	
233	   ### 🟢 During {next phase} — informational
234	   4. ...
235	   ```
236	
237	   Items the counterparty owes the user belong as "wait for X" items, not as user-owned tasks. Items the user owes belong as imperative bullets with reasoning the user could repeat to a third party.
238	
239	When the meeting is purely informational (e.g. a recruiter screen with no clear next step from the user side), skip the second part and just deliver the status line. Use judgment — meetings that resolved a contentious open question, drove a decline/accept decision, or unblocked an active project virtually always warrant the action-items list.
240	
241	## Anti-Patterns
242	
243	- Creating the meeting page without enriching attendees
244	- Skipping entity propagation ("I'll do that later")
245	- Not merging timelines across all mentioned entities
246	- Creating attendee stubs without meaningful content
247	- Filing meeting pages without cross-linking to all participants
248	- Slugging entities from a typo'd filename without verifying the spelling against the recruiter email / company website (see Phase 1)
249	- Treating a header-only transcript stub as an error instead of reconstructing the meeting from adjacent sources (see Phase 1)
250	- Asking the user to paste an email they referenced when you can retrieve it via gog (see `references/email-retrieval.md`)
251	- Relying on cached read_file output for a source transcript after the user said "I added the transcript" or otherwise indicated they updated the file — re-read and resynth (see Phase 1)
252	- Silently normalizing a recruiter's or founder's numeric claim (basis points, comp range, valuation, headcount) instead of flagging the discrepancy verbatim in the brain page (see Phase 1)
253	- Paraphrasing the exchange that drove the user's downstream action (decline, accept, escalate) instead of preserving the verbatim quote (see Phase 1)
254	- Anchoring on the first or most-elaborated option in a multi-option transcript passage and missing the resolution that picked a different option (see Phase 1)
255	- Treating joint-pronoun language ("we hold them responsible", "you, me", "between us") as rhetorical when it is structural — it usually means both parties are in the accountability chain (see Phase 1)
256	- Not re-reading the decision-relevant passage against the draft meeting page before propagating to entity pages — financial/contractual terms (markups, fees, who-holds-the-contract) are the highest-value places to double-check (see Phase 1)
257	- Surface-fixing only the most-recently-touched page when the user corrects a misread fact, instead of propagating across every page that references the fact in a single ✏️ fix commit (see Phase 1)
258	- Bundling `gbrain check-backlinks fix` hygiene edits on unrelated pages into a content commit instead of a separate `🔗 link` commit (see Phase 7)
259	- Asking the user where the new transcripts are when `git status` would have shown them as untracked files in `sources/transcripts/` (see Phase 0)
260	- Ingesting a meeting that had a prep doc without reconciling the two — dropping the "which prepped questions got answered / what's still open" analysis and leaving the prep with no forward link to its outcome (see Phase 2.5)
261	- Ending a synth with only the meeting page and status line when the meeting drove a downstream user decision — the user-facing prioritized action items list (Output Format part 2) is mandatory in that case
262	
263	## Linked references
264	
265	- `references/email-retrieval.md` — retrieve referenced gmail threads via gog and convert them into source pages.
266
